issues.legal_issue: A land acquisition for a charitable organization is not mala fide merely because the organization changes the stated project after its initial application when the evidence shows a genuine need for the land and no collateral purpose.
material_facts: The organization first sought land to expand a dispensary, but an inquiry found it was not then operating one.
It later sought a larger area for social workers’ quarters, a students’ home, a publication department, a guest house and a panthasala.
The organization’s available accommodation was inadequate, its activities were overcrowded or restricted, and the record supported its need for additional space.
The landowners produced no evidence that the stated purposes were not genuine or that the government acted to assist the organization for a collateral purpose.
issues.conclusion: The allegation that the acquisition proceedings were commenced mala fide was not sustained.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the alleged bad faith against the record of the organization’s charitable and philanthropic activities and its genuine need for additional accommodation; it relied on no particular statutory provision or earlier case for this conclusion.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A landowner challenged a government acquisition on the ground that it was undertaken in bad faith.
predicates.genuine_need_for_land: The acquiring organization had a genuine need for additional land to carry on or expand its activities.
predicates.no_evidence_of_collateral_purpose: The challenger produced no evidence that the stated acquisition purpose was unreal or that the government acted for a collateral purpose.

issues.definition: When a challenged acquisition is supported by a genuine need or the challenger produces no evidence of a collateral purpose, the acquisition is not mala fide.

issues.legal_issue: Under the company-acquisition requirements before their amendment, acquisition for a company to construct works was invalid if the works were not directly usable by the public as of right and the agreement did not secure such public use.
material_facts: The land was acquired for a registered society and the entire compensation was to be paid from the society’s funds.
The proposed facilities were not works directly usable by the public as of right.
The agreement did not covenant that the public would have a right to use the works directly.
The acquisition therefore did not satisfy the requirements then applicable to acquisition for a company.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition could not be sustained under the Land Acquisition Act as it stood before the 1962 amendment.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 39, 40(1)(b) and 41(5) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, read together, a work acquired for a company had to be directly useful to the public through the public’s right to use the work itself, and the agreement had to provide for the public’s entitlement to use it. The Court applied the first R. L. Arora v. State of U.P., 1962 (S2) SCR 149; AIR 1962 SC 764.

rule.if: company_land_acquisition_challenge and compensation_paid_by_company and work_not_directly_usable_by_public and agreement_lacks_public_right_of_direct_use

predicates.company_land_acquisition_challenge: A landowner challenged an acquisition made for a company or other entity treated as a company for acquisition purposes.
predicates.compensation_paid_by_company: The company or acquiring entity was to pay the entire acquisition compensation.
predicates.work_not_directly_usable_by_public: The work to be built was not itself directly usable by the public as of right.
predicates.agreement_lacks_public_right_of_direct_u: The agreement did not give the public a right to use the work directly.

issues.definition: An acquisition for a company fails under the original requirements when the company pays the compensation, the work is not directly usable by the public, and the agreement gives the public no right to use it directly.

issues.legal_issue: A pre-amendment acquisition for a company is validated retrospectively when the acquired land is for buildings or works that support the public-purpose work of an entity pursuing such a purpose, the government’s satisfaction and consent are established, and the agreement provides for construction conditions.
material_facts: The acquisition was completed before the 1962 amendment and was for a registered society treated as a company under the Act.
The society pursued charitable, religious and philanthropic activities that served public purposes, including relief for people in need and support for education and medical institutions.
The society was short of space, and the record showed that the proposed quarters, students’ home, publication department, guest house and panthasala would facilitate its activities.
The government’s satisfaction and consent were supported by the acquisition inquiry and the agreement with the society.
The agreement restricted the land to the identified purposes and required completion and equipping of the facilities within a specified time, with a right of re-entry in case of non-compliance.
issues.conclusion: The retrospective amendment applied, the acquisition satisfied its requirements, and the acquisition was valid.
issues.legal_principle: Section 40(1)(aa), Section 41(4-A), and Section 7 of the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1962, permit and retrospectively validate acquisition for a building or work for a company engaged in an industry or work for a public purpose when the building or work subserves that public-purpose activity and the agreement addresses construction conditions. The Court applied the second R. L. Arora v. State of U.P., 1964 AIR SC 1230. It distinguished State of West Bengal v. P. N. Talukdar, 1965 AIR SC 646, because the evidence there did not establish the necessary connection between the buildings and the public-purpose work. The Court also treated public purpose broadly, consistent with Babu Barkya Thakur v. State of Bombay, 1961 (1) SCR 128; AIR 1960 SC 1203, while noting that the earlier company-acquisition provisions required direct public use under the first Arora case.

rule.if: company_land_acquisition and acquisition_preceded_retroactive_change and entity_pursued_public_purpose_work and proposed_buildings_subserved_that_work and government_satisfaction_and_consent_evidenced and agreement_specified_construction_conditions

predicates.company_land_acquisition: The land was acquired for an entity treated as a company for land-acquisition purposes.
predicates.acquisition_preceded_retroactive_change: The acquisition was made before a later legal change that applied retrospectively to such acquisitions.
predicates.entity_pursued_public_purpose_work: The acquiring entity was engaged in work serving a public purpose.
predicates.proposed_buildings_subserved_that_work: The proposed buildings or works facilitated the entity’s public-purpose activities.
predicates.government_satisfaction_and_consent_evid: The record, including inquiry materials or the agreement, showed that the government was satisfied about and consented to the qualifying purpose.
predicates.agreement_specified_construction_conditi: The agreement set out conditions governing the construction or execution of the proposed buildings or works.

issues.definition: A pre-change company acquisition is valid when the acquiring entity pursued public-purpose work, the proposed buildings served that work, the government’s satisfaction and consent are evidenced, and the agreement set construction conditions.

issues.legal_issue: When compliance with the requirements for an acquisition for a company is challenged, the company or government must establish the acquisition’s validity, and government satisfaction and consent may be proved from the agreement, inquiry materials or other evidence.
material_facts: The landowners challenged the acquisition on the ground that the requirements governing acquisition for a company had not been met.

The acquisition record included an inquiry report, evidence of the society’s need for accommodation, the government’s consent, and an agreement limiting the land to the stated purposes and providing for construction.
The Court found that the evidence abundantly established the government’s satisfaction and consent in this case.
issues.conclusion: The burden of establishing validity lay on the company or government, and the evidence in this case discharged it.
issues.legal_principle: The Court stated that the question whether the appropriate government was satisfied about a qualifying purpose and consented to acquisition is a question of fact to be decided on the evidence in each case. Satisfaction and consent may be established through recitals in the agreement under Section 41, a report under Section 5-A, the result of an inquiry under Section 40(2), or other evidence. The Court distinguished State of West Bengal v. P. N. Talukdar, 1965 AIR SC 646, where it was not satisfied that the necessary government satisfaction had been established.

predicates.company_land_acquisition_challenge: A landowner challenged whether an acquisition made for a company complied with the applicable acquisition requirements.

issues.definition: When a landowner challenges an acquisition for a company, the company or government must establish that the acquisition was valid.
